name: singleton
intent: Guarantee that a type or module has exactly one instance in its scope and give clients a well-known access point to it, so a genuinely single resource is shared instead of duplicated.
problem: A resource must exist exactly once per process (one configuration, one pool, one cache, one device handle, one registry) and must be reachable from code that has no natural injection point. Duplicating it splits state — two caches, two locks, two divergent copies of the same table — while a plain global neither enforces the uniqueness nor defines when the instance is constructed.
context: Applies when uniqueness is an observable property of the problem rather than a convenience: one device or OS resource, a process-wide table that must stay consistent, or a service whose construction is expensive and should happen lazily. It becomes urgent under concurrency, because the lazy construction itself must happen exactly once across threads, and it becomes misleading in systems where 'one' is really per class loader, per worker or isolate, per Ractor or per replica.
benefits: Uniqueness is enforced by the type or the module instead of by convention, so clients cannot accidentally construct a second instance and the invariant cannot drift.
One well-known access point, usable from code that has no constructor to inject through: entry points, framework callbacks, device glue.

Lazy first-use construction: an expensive resource is built only if it is needed, at a deterministic point (first access) rather than at startup, which also sidesteps static-initialisation-order problems.
Shared caches, pools and registries keep one consistent state exactly where the problem demands it instead of silently forking per call site.
An existing single real-world resource (one spooler, one audio channel, one license, one hardware device) is made explicit in the design rather than being an implicit global.
The instance is created once and handed out cheaply, so per-call construction cost disappears where the object is genuinely reusable.
tradeoffs: Global mutable state in disguise: any code can reach the instance, so dependencies stay invisible in signatures and APIs end up lying about what they need.

Test isolation breaks down: the instance survives across tests and cannot be substituted, so suites grow reset()/setForTest()/instance-replacement hacks, cannot isolate parts, and cannot hold two configurations at once.
Lifetime belongs to the process, not to a caller: resources held by the singleton are released only at exit (or never, for statics whose destructors do not run), and teardown order is unspecified.

Thread-safe lazy initialisation is genuinely hard: double-checked locking is unreliable without a memory-model guarantee (pre-C++11 C++, pre-Java-5 Java), so every implementation has to get a memory-model detail right.

Construction that can fail or needs parameters does not fit a static accessor: retrying a failed initialisation, reconfiguring, or running two deployments of the same code in one process all become awkward.

'One' is only as strong as the runtime's unit of uniqueness — class loader, dynamic library, worker or isolate, Ractor, replica — and code that assumes per-machine uniqueness breaks silently when that unit changes.
Removing the access point later is invasive: once call sites depend on a global accessor, reintroducing explicit dependencies means touching all of them.

The Borg pattern (shared state, many instances) is a more flexible Python-native alternative that avoids identity coupling while still giving all instances the same state; it is listed as an alias but is conceptually distinct.

participants.responsibility: Defines the access operation (instance()/Instance/Get) that returns the unique instance, holds it, and forbids every other creation path through a private constructor, module-private state, or an enforced module boundary.
Reach the instance solely through the access operation; they must not construct, clone, deserialise or otherwise manufacture a second instance.

use_cases: Process-wide configuration or settings, loaded once from a file or the environment and read on nearly every request.
A shared connection pool, thread pool or network client whose duplication would exhaust the external resource or split its accounting.
One handle to a physical or OS-level singleton: printer spooler, audio channel, serial port, graphics context, license token.
A process-wide logger or metrics sink, where losing or reordering events because two instances exist is worse than global access.
An authoritative in-memory registry or catalog (plugin registrations, feature flags, schema cache) that must have exactly one copy.
An embedded interpreter or native library handle that may be initialised only once per process and must not be re-entered.

A distributed-service singleton in a replicated system where exactly one replica holds a leadership lock or serves as the primary — but this requires a distributed coordination layer (etcd, ZooKeeper, Redis) and is not enforced by the pattern alone.
A hardware peripheral handle where the OS or driver permits exactly one open handle at a time, and opening a second fails or aliases the first.

java.lang.Runtime in the JDK itself: no public constructor, one Runtime per application handed out solely by Runtime.getRuntime(), wrapping a genuinely single resource — the live runtime environment (availableProcessors(), exit(), memory queries).

Apple Foundation/UIKit's shared-instance convention: UIApplication.shared (created at launch by UIApplicationMain), URLSession.shared and FileManager.default are framework-provided singletons; the shared URLSession deliberately shares caches, cookies and credentials, and Apple documents dropping to a custom instance when that shared state must be isolated.

Node.js CommonJS module cache as the module-scope singleton: module.exports IS the instance — require() returns the identical object for the same resolved filename, which is why duplicate installs under different resolved paths silently yield two 'singletons'.
avoid_when: A composition root can create exactly one instance and hand it to the few consumers — use constructor injection and get uniqueness for free.
The object should be one per request, tenant, thread or test — use DI-container lifetimes, a registry or multiton, or thread-local storage, not a process-wide accessor.
The type is stateless or the behaviour is pure — use a module of free functions or an object of statics; shared identity adds nothing.
The value is immutable and small — a constant or value object is simpler and cannot be mutated under you.
A framework already owns lifetimes (Spring @Component, .NET DI, NestJS providers, Rails initialisers) — register a singleton-scoped service and inject it instead of adding a static access point.
The only reason is to avoid threading a parameter through a call chain — that is convenience, not a uniqueness requirement; fix the call chain or introduce a facade/service boundary.
anti_patterns: Singleton as a convenience global: reaching for the accessor purely to avoid passing a dependency, producing invisible dependency graphs.
Bolt-on testability: reset(), setForTest() or a reflection-based instance replacement added to the singleton class — it is the design, not the test, that needs the seam.
Double-checked locking copied onto toolchains without the required memory-model guarantee (pre-C++11, pre-Java-5, or C without atomics).
Unqualified uniqueness: claiming one instance per system when the runtime provides one per class loader, worker, Ractor or replica, so the singleton silently multiplies.
Kitchen-sink singleton: one instance that also accumulates unrelated caches, preferences and counters because it is reachable anyway.
Eager chains: every singleton constructing every other at startup through static accessors, turning first use into an order-dependent startup graph.
Eternal singleton: a singleton that never releases held resources because the language (e.g., static destructor in C++, module-level state in Python) never calls a destructor at process exit.

Distributed singleton illusion: claiming per-system uniqueness in a microservices architecture where each service instance initialises its own local singleton, silently creating duplicate state without cross-process synchronisation.
design_principles: Enforce an invariant where it cannot be bypassed: uniqueness belongs to the type (closed construction) or to the module (module-scope state), not to documentation.
Depend on abstractions: clients should depend on an interface they could substitute; the singleton should implement it and be injected wherever injection is possible.
Separate construction from use: uniqueness and lifetime are one responsibility, and mixing them with the resource's own behaviour or with per-request state breaks both.
Prefer explicit dependencies over hidden ones: passing the instance is the default; a global access point needs a justification such as a missing injection point or a real device singleton.
Least knowledge: the accessor exposes the instance, not a back door to every collaborator of the module.
Own your lifetime: if the singleton holds resources, document when and how they are released; prefer RAII, scoped guards, or explicit close() to relying on process exit.
best_practices: Default to a container- or DI-managed single instance and keep the static access point for the narrow cases that have no injection path.

Make lazy construction thread-safe with the sanctioned primitive of the language — C++11 function-local static (Meyers' Singleton), Java enum or volatile double-check, C# Lazy<T>, Python threading.Lock around module init, Rust std::sync::OnceLock or LazyLock, Go sync.Once — instead of hand-rolled double-checked locking.
Close the bypasses: private constructor or module-private state, deleted copy/move, and guards against clone, deserialisation and reflection where a second instance can be manufactured that way.
Document what 'one' means (process, class loader, worker, replica) and what happens when construction fails, including whether a retry is possible.
Keep the instance immutable or explicitly synchronised; shared mutable state with no owner is the real hazard, not the accessor itself.
Provide a deliberate test seam: inject the instance where possible, or return it from a swappable provider so tests can substitute or reset it without reflection.

In Python, prefer module-level state (the module is already a singleton) over a class-based singleton, or use the Borg pattern when identity is irrelevant but shared state is required — it avoids the rigidity of private constructors while remaining simple.

In Python, the cleanest lazy-accessor form is `functools.cache` on a module-level function or `@classmethod` + `@functools.cache` on the class — simpler than a class-based singleton and avoids `__new__` gymnastics.

In C++, the only correct singleton form in modern C++ is the function-local static (Meyers' Singleton); class-static member init is not thread-safe pre-C++11 and the double-checked locking pattern is unnecessary post-C++11.
In DI-framework environments (.NET, Spring, NestJS), configure singleton scope at the container level rather than coding it into the class — the framework owns lifetime, not the class.

Audit the singleton surface area regularly: a singleton that accumulates caches, registries, and configuration makes it difficult to reason about memory and state; decompose it into focused services that can be injected.

In Python, use the 3-step migration path to testability: (1) replace eager module-level objects with a cached `get_instance()` function + `cache_clear()` for reset, (2) add a swappable override global so tests can inject a double without patching, (3) pass the instance explicitly via constructor injection at the composition root.

In Python 3.13+ with free-threading enabled, explicit `threading.Lock` around lazy construction is essential — the GIL previously masked race conditions, and free-threaded mode exposes them; always synchronise shared mutable state.
In Python, `functools.cache` on an accessor with parameters caches per distinct argument tuple; call `cache_clear()` in test teardown or between test cases to prevent cross-test contamination.

Avoid `importlib.reload()` as a singleton reset mechanism — it re-executes module code, producing a new state dictionary rather than resetting the original; clients holding references to the old state survive the reload.

Brett L. Schuchert, 'DIP in the Wild', martinfowler.com, 2013 — DI, IoC, DIP distinctions and their interaction with singletons in real systems.

Alex Martelli & David Ascher, 'Avoiding the Singleton Design Pattern with the Borg Idiom', Python Cookbook, 3rd ed. (O'Reilly) — Borg implementation, subclassing semantics, new-style class compatibility; distinction from GoF Singleton.

Ned Batchelder, 'Singleton is a Bad Idea', nedbatchelder.com, 2022 — why singletons lie about their nature; functools.cache as cleaner alternative; module-level instances; tests can still create fresh instances when needed.

PTD / python-testing-debugging.com, 'Replacing Singletons and Module Globals in Tests', 2026-08 — three-step migration path (lazy accessor, explicit override seam, full injection); module-level object rebinding mechanics; functools.cache gotchas; autouse fixture for cross-test leak detection.

IN-COM DATA SYSTEMS, 'Modern Singleton Strategies for Cloud-Native and Distributed Architectures', 2025-10 — distributed singleton anti-patterns when migrating monoliths to microservices; per-service-instance singleton vs. cross-service coordination; external state stores; service mesh as non-invasive alternative.

Clean Code Guy (Martin Adams), 'Singleton Pattern: Use, Pitfalls & Alternatives', 2026-01 — coupling metrics (afferent coupling 6.86 vs 3.35 for stateful singletons); when singletons are acceptable; ES Modules as natural singleton in JS/TS; DI vs. module exports comparison table.

ArchMan (archman.dev), 'Singleton Pattern', 2026 — decision flowchart (genuine single instance? DI possible? hardware constraint?); Bill Pugh/Holder pattern; thread-local singleton; service registry as alternative; microservices warning.

Ankush Choudhary Johal, 'Refactoring Singleton Patterns to Dependency Injection', johal.in, 2026-03 — real-world MedTrack case study; three-step refactoring with automated tests; circular dependencies, missing dependencies, and state management during migration.

faif/python-patterns, 'Borg pattern', github.com/faif/python-patterns — modern Python 3 Borg implementation using `_shared_state` class attribute and `__init__` rebinding; subclass state isolation; doctest demonstrating shared vs. distinct identity.

(2009, updated) — subclassing semantics differ: Borg subclasses share state with parent unless they override `_shared_state`; Singleton subclasses get independent instances; Borg allows optional non-shared instantiation via constructor parameter.

Oracle JDK API Specification: java.lang.Runtime — each Java application has a single Runtime instance, accessible only via getRuntime(); the canonical single-resource handle (availableProcessors, exit, memory): https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Runtime.html.

Apple Developer Documentation: UIApplication.shared — the shared singleton app object created automatically at launch by UIApplicationMain, cited with URLSession.shared and FileManager.default as framework singletons: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/uiapplication/shared.

Apple Developer Documentation: URLSession.shared — the shared singleton session needing no configuration or delegate; it shares default caches, cookies and credentials, so custom caching/auth requires an isolated session: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/urlsession/shared.

Apple Developer Documentation: FileManager — FileManager.default is the standard shared instance, thread-safe for general use; delegate-based move/copy notifications require a dedicated instance: https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/filemanager.

Node.js Documentation: Modules (CommonJS) — modules are cached after first load, so repeated require() of the same resolved filename returns the identical module.exports object; deleting require.cache entries forces re-instantiation, and different resolved filenames yield distinct cached modules: https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html.

Java Object Serialization Specification §3 (Object Input Classes) — readResolve replaces a deserialised object with a pre-existing instance to preserve singleton/canonical identity; enum constants are deserialised by name via Enum.valueOf, ignoring readObject/readResolve, making enum singletons inherently stable: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/serialization/input.html.

Kenton Varda, 'Singletons Considered Harmful', kentonshouse.com — singletons as disguised global variables with hard-coded dependencies; environment pattern and explicit parameter passing as the alternatives: https://kentonshouse.com/singletons.
